The image in a concave mirror appears upside down because of how light rays converge after reflecting off the mirror's surface. When parallel rays of light hit the concave mirror, they reflect and converge at a point called the focal point. If the object is placed beyond the focal point, the reflected rays diverge and create an image that is inverted (upside down) compared to the object. This occurs due to the geometry of the mirror and the path of the light rays. 

Can you think about what happens to the rays when the object is placed beyond the focal point? (Sec 9.2.3)

The focal length (f) of a concave mirror is considered negative because of the sign convention used in optics, specifically the Cartesian sign convention. In this convention, distances measured in the direction of the incoming light (toward the mirror) are taken as negative, while distances measured in the opposite direction (away from the mirror) are positive.

For a concave mirror, the focal point (F) is located in front of the mirror, where parallel rays of light converge after reflection. Since this point is on the same side as the incoming light, it is assigned a negative value. Therefore, the focal length of a concave mirror is negative. This is a standard practice in optics to maintain consistency in calculations and understanding of image formation.
